How the ACL is enforced

Method, as implemented in acl_firewall.py and the controller

Rules are data, loaded from a JSON file: each rule carries a priority (higher wins), source and destination CIDRs, a protocol, optional source and destination ports or port ranges, and an action. The engine checks the classic 5-tuple in priority order and returns the winning rule's action; the default policy applies when no rule matches. Loading validates every CIDR, port range, protocol and action, so a rules file that loads is a rules file that was validated.

In the controller, the check runs on access-switch packet-ins (after the slicing check, before QoS classification). A deny installs a drop flow for that flow, so repeated packets stop reaching the controller, and logs an acl_drop control event naming the winning rule — the recorded drops on this page are those events, aggregated across the live captures and the campaign recordings, with the rule index parsed back out of each logged reason.

The engine in the controller counts hits per rule in its own process; those counters are not written to disk, so this page does not invent them. What it shows instead are probes: packets constructed from the rules themselves and evaluated by a fresh engine when the page is requested, with that engine's hit counts reported as probe counts.
